title: Hunger, Fatigue and Big Plans. Why Is It So Hard to Predict Our Own Decisions?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.
sources: Buehler, Roger; Griffin, Dale; Ross, Michael, Exploring the “Planning Fallacy”: Why People Underestimate Their Task Completion Times, “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology” 67 (1994)
Kahneman, Daniel, Thinking, Fast and Slow, Farrar, Straus and Giroux 2011
Read, Daniel; van Leeuwen, Barbara, Predicting Hunger: The Effects of Appetite and Delay on Choice, “Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes” 76 (1998)
Wenham, Gordon J., Genesis 16–50, Word Biblical Commentary 2, Word Books 1994
Xu, Alison Jing; Schwarz, Norbert; Wyer, Robert S., Hunger Promotes Acquisition of Nonfood Objects, “Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences” 112 (2015)

paragraphs: One day the British researcher Daniel Read offered office workers a free snack: they could choose a piece of fruit or a chocolate bar. Everyone placed their order a week in advance, but after seven days they could still change their mind just before the food was handed out. The result was telling: when the treat was to be in their hands “in a moment”, the unhealthy option won far more often than when they were planning “for next week”. What is more, people who were hungry when they ordered chose the chocolate bar much more often, even when the snack was to reach them at a time when they expected to be full. The present state of the body was shaping decisions about the future.

We plan our time and money in exactly the same way. We usually draw up the household budget with an ideal in mind, a month without surprises, and we set deadlines for an imaginary week in which nobody comes down with flu. Yet simply being aware of these mechanisms does not protect us from them; only a change of approach helps. That is why it is better to plan your grocery shopping on a full stomach, and when you set a completion date for a new task, be sure to check how long something similar took you last time.

The book of Genesis tells of Esau, who came back from the field exhausted just as his brother Jacob was cooking a meal. Esau doesn’t even ask what the dish is; he just blurts out: “Give me that red stuff” (in the original Hebrew the phrase sounds blunter than in English translations). In return Jacob demands the rights of the firstborn son, which in this family were bound up with the great promise given to Abraham. Esau replies: “I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me?” (Genesis 25:32). From where he stood, it sounded like a sensible calculation, except that Esau was not dying at all; he was simply very tired. He ate, drank, got up and went away, and only at the very end does the narrator reveal that what had been bubbling in the pot was ordinary lentils.

Esau was no fool, but a man for whom the present completely blotted out the future. Anyone knows this who, worn out at midnight, has bought something on impulse or promised the boss an unrealistic report by Friday, and in the morning looked at their own decision in utter disbelief.

Psalm 103, however, reminds us of a God who knows this human frailty inside out. He has compassion on us as a father has compassion on his children, because He remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:13–14). The Creator knows our tiredness and does not despise us for it. At the same time, He teaches us to look further than our next meal. Wisdom, then, means making key decisions in a good hour, and in a bad one holding firmly to what has already been decided.
Prepared by: Marek Micyk
Content editor: Beata Dutkowska

questions: Which of my desires today will turn out, a week from now, to be nothing more than a bowl of lentil stew?
challenge: Before you put down your phone or close your computer today, recall one purchase or one promise from the last few days that you made when you were tired, hungry, or when it was already late at night. Admit to yourself what exactly you were feeling at the time: was it plain hunger, exhaustion, or perhaps a craving for instant reward?

paragraphs: When will you hand in your thesis? That was the question the Canadian psychologist Roger Buehler and his team put by phone to thirty-seven psychology students at the University of Waterloo. All of them were in their final semester, and their projects were already well advanced. Each was asked to give the most accurate, realistic date by which the finished text would be submitted. Then they were asked for a second date, one that allowed for a worst-case scenario in which things would not go their way.

On average the students gave themselves thirty-four days to finish writing, and their worst-case scenario assumed forty-nine. Life, however, overturned these plans with interest: in the end the theses were handed in after an average of fifty-five days. Fewer than three in ten students managed to finish by the date they themselves had considered realistic.

And yet these young people knew their subject, since they had spent several years learning how the human mind works. In a separate questionnaire completed as part of the same study, the students admitted that they had handed in roughly two thirds of their previous assignments later than they had planned. They were fully aware of their past experience, and still, when planning the next task, they believed that this time everything would go smoothly.

The same mechanism can be seen in larger projects too. According to estimates made in 1957, the Sydney Opera House was to be ready in early 1963 and cost 7 million dollars. In the end it was opened only in 1973, and in a scaled-down version that still cost 102 million. Your bathroom renovation will at most become a family anecdote, but it is governed by exactly the same logic.
So why do intelligent, experienced people get time and money wrong so stubbornly?

sections.heading: A Plan Written on a Good Day
paragraphs: When you plan, you look at the task only “from the inside”: you focus on the successive steps and assume that each one will go the way you want. What you don’t take into account is the flu that will catch you in the third week of writing, or the supervisor who will get back to you only after ten days. Each of these obstacles on its own seems unlikely, but the more of them you allow for, the greater the chance that at least one will happen and upset your plans.

Buehler’s team checked what helps correct this excessive optimism. This time the researchers gave the students a slightly different challenge. They were to estimate when they would finish their work if this time it went exactly as their previous projects had. Only when the participants were made to connect the new plan with their delays from past years did their forecasts become more realistic. Until then that knowledge had been useless, because the students explained away earlier delays as plain bad luck or an unusual run of circumstances. They treated the past as a one-off mishap, not as a steady rule.

Even professional researchers of thinking errors are not immune to this, as the psychologist and Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman recounted with disarming honesty. In Israel he once put together a team to write a textbook for secondary schools on sound judgment and decision-making. After a year of weekly meetings he asked everyone to write down on a slip of paper how much more time they needed to finish the project. The answers hovered around two years. Then Kahneman asked the curriculum expert in the group how other teams had fared with similar projects. After a moment’s thought, the man admitted with embarrassment that about forty percent of the groups had never finished the work, and none of the rest had completed it in less than seven years. Interestingly, the same man had just written an equally optimistic forecast on his own slip of paper. Even so, the team carried on as if nothing had happened, and the textbook went to print only eight years later.

This phenomenon has another side, though. In a further study by Buehler, observers estimated how long a task would take a complete stranger, and as a rule they allowed more time than the person actually needed. We judge others by how things usually go, but ourselves by how perfectly they could go.

The same mechanism governs our wallets. According to a survey carried out in 2002, Americans who were remodeling their kitchens expected to spend an average of just under 19,000 dollars. Reality harshly corrected these plans, and the final bill came to an average of almost 39,000. We usually draw up our monthly budget with the ideal scenario in mind, while almost every month brings some surprise. One time it is a family birthday, another time a fine or a sudden trip to the dentist. We treat each of these expenses on its own as an exception to the rule, even though taken together they make up a steady monthly reality.

sections.heading: A Chocolate Bar for Next Week
paragraphs: Planning, in any case, is only one of many areas in which our minds go wrong in such predictable ways. Another trap lies even closer, right by the checkout.

In an experiment published in 1998, the British researcher Daniel Read and his colleague Barbara van Leeuwen offered office workers a free snack. They could choose fruit or something far less healthy: a chocolate bar, crisps or peanuts. Each person chose in advance the snack they would receive exactly one week later. When the researchers came back a week later with the order, they let the participants change their minds just before the food was handed out. The result was telling: when people chose “for now”, the unhealthy snacks won far more often than when they planned “for next week”. The same people who made sensible decisions from a distance reached for the chocolate bar when the moment came.

The researchers also checked one more relationship. Some people placed their order right after lunch, while the rest did so late in the afternoon, when their stomachs had long been empty. The hungry workers chose unhealthy snacks much more often. Interestingly, they did so even when the food was to reach them a week later at a time when, as they well knew, they would be full. The present state of the body inevitably shaped decisions about the future. Researchers have called this phenomenon an empathy gap with our own selves: someone who has eaten cannot imagine being hungry, and someone who is hungry cannot remember at all what it is like to be full.

More than a decade later, a team led by Alison Jing Xu showed that hunger changes even our attitude to things that cannot be eaten at all. Hungry participants in the experiment took more free office paper clips, and on real shopping trips they also spent more on non-food items. Interestingly, they liked the paper clips exactly as much as people who had eaten; they simply wanted more of them. Although this is a single publication and it is unwise to build far-reaching theories on it, it fits perfectly with the experience of anyone who has ever gone shopping right before lunch.

Our resistance to temptation also drops sharply when it is late and we are tired. That is exactly when we become defenseless against manipulation. All it takes is a late hour and a screen with a pulsing countdown reading “offer ends in 2:14:37”. Although such a clock tells us nothing about the quality of the shoes we happen to be looking at, it can effectively overshadow every rational argument and push us to tap “Buy now”.

sections.heading: That Red Stuff, That Red Stuff
paragraphs: The book of Genesis tells the story of twin brothers. Esau grew up to be an excellent hunter and a man of the open country, while the quiet Jacob stayed among the tents (Genesis 25:27). One day Jacob was preparing a meal when Esau came back from the field completely exhausted. The smell of food hung in the air, and something red was bubbling in the pot.

Esau doesn’t even ask what the dish is. He says he is worn out and asks for “some of that red stew” (Genesis 25:30), although in the original Hebrew it sounds much blunter, something like: “give me that red stuff, that red stuff”. The word is repeated, as if the exhausted man could no longer call things by their names and saw only the color. The narrator adds that this is where his later nickname Edom, meaning “Red”, came from. What was really bubbling in the pot we learn only in the last sentence of the scene: it was ordinary lentils.

Jacob already has his price ready. He demands the birthright, which in that world meant the right to a double portion of the father’s estate (Deuteronomy 21:17) and the position of the future head of the clan. In this particular family, however, far more was at stake: it was through the elder son that the great promise given to Abraham was to be carried forward.

Esau’s reply sounds surprisingly reasonable: “I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me?” (Genesis 25:32). From the inside it was a perfectly logical calculation: what use is an inheritance thirty years from now if you are going to die tonight? Except that Esau was not dying at all; he was simply tired after a whole day in the field. It was the present state of his body that handed him an argument which at that moment seemed impossible to refute.

Then the story clearly speeds up. Jacob demands an oath and hands over bread and lentils, and Esau eats, drinks, gets up and goes away. Four verbs one after another, without a word of comment. A scene that decided the future of a whole family line lasted as long as a single meal. Only at the very end does the narrator allow himself a verdict: “Thus Esau despised his birthright” (Genesis 25:34).

Jacob does not come out of this spotless either. He saw the value of the birthright, and even before the twins were born the LORD had told their mother that the older would serve the younger (Genesis 25:23), yet he lacked patience. Instead of trusting that God Himself would see to it, Jacob decided to settle the matter over the cooking pot by exploiting his own brother’s weakness. But the book of Genesis knows no perfect heroes. In it God works with people exactly as they are, and He fulfills His promises in spite of their selfish calculations.

Centuries later, the author of the Letter to the Hebrews returns to this scene and mentions Esau, “who for a single meal sold his birthright” (Hebrews 12:16). He sets him against a long gallery of people of faith. Of them he had written earlier that they did not live to receive what was promised, but saw it and welcomed it from afar (Hebrews 11:13). The contrast is striking: Abraham lived by what he could not yet see clearly, while his grandson Esau lived by what was steaming under his nose.

sections.heading: The God Who Knows What We Are Made Of
paragraphs: It is easy to turn Esau’s story into a moralizing fable about the foolish brother, yet the biblical text tells it in a far more balanced way. Esau was simply an utterly exhausted man for whom the present completely blotted out the future. It is exactly the same mechanism that makes you buy a third pair of shoes at midnight and, in the morning, has you promising your boss the report by Friday.

Research also points to one uncomfortable truth: knowing about illusions does not in itself protect us from them. The psychology students had years of studying the mind behind them and were aware of their own earlier delays, yet their plans were still wildly optimistic. Understanding the mechanism changes nothing on its own; only a change of approach helps. So before you name your next deadline for a task, check exactly how long it took you last time, and let that number be your starting point. And set your rules and budgets only when nothing is distracting you: not hunger, not tiredness, not a countdown ticking on the screen.

These mechanisms lay bare the truth about human nature. We are beings of flesh and blood, and our bodies constantly influence every thought we have. Psalm 103 describes a God who knows this frailty inside out. “As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him. For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust” (Psalm 103:13–14). God knows your tiredness and your hunger. He knows how they affect you, and He does not despise your human weakness.

There is also a deep lesson about faith here. In the Letter to the Hebrews, faith means the ability to look much further than your next meal. Such a perspective grows on calm days, built on a relationship with Someone who sees incomparably more than you do. In the moment of testing and fatigue we can only draw on the reserves we managed to gather beforehand. True wisdom, then, lies in making key decisions in a good hour, and in a bad one holding on to what has already been decided.

Anyone who knows that shopping temptations are harder to resist in the evening does not have to fight heroic battles with themselves; it is enough to close the shopping app before ten at night. Anyone who knows that optimism carries them away when planning can simply add a generous time buffer to every deadline. This advice may not sound very spiritual, and yet at heart it is a form of deep humility: accepting that we are only human, not infallible robots.
Prepared by: Marek Micyk
Content editor: Beata Dutkowska

questions: Which of my desires today will turn out, a week from now, to be nothing more than a bowl of lentil stew?
challenge: **In your thoughts.** Recall one purchase or one promise from the last few days that you made under the influence of tiredness, hunger or a late hour. Admit to yourself what exactly you were feeling at the time: was it plain hunger, exhaustion, or perhaps a craving for instant reward?

**In action.** Today, open your bank account history or go through your receipts from the last thirty days. Mark three expenses you would not repeat now. Next to each one, note exactly what time it was made and what state you were in. If you spot a recurring pattern, such as online shopping in the evenings, set one simple rule for the coming month. It might be: “After 10 p.m. I don’t buy anything; the basket waits until morning.” Write it somewhere you will see it, even as your computer wallpaper. And if you don’t have your account history to hand, do exactly the same with your calendar, only this time pick three deadlines you recently failed to meet.
